profile.headline: Java Artificer
profile.summary:
Java software architect specializing in secure enterprise infrastructure, and reusable software (web and database frameworks, graphics tools, utility libraries … whatever reduces duplicated effort, bugs and inefficiencies). Java specialist since JDK 1.1, with perspective informed by long C and assembly background. Like understanding systems at bit & byte level, so can “see” Java data structure memory footprints, read bytecode, understand character sets/encodings, transcoding and transliteration, and enjoy reading JDK source and JEPs. Develop concurrent and parallel software. Analyze and design SQL databases. Emphasize communication quality, especially in technical writing and API design. Provide direct, ongoing support to end-users and developers for all projects. Work both independently, and in diverse teams.

Built, applied and honed those skills serving the State of Texas for 33 years at Texas Workforce Commission (TWC), and University of Texas at Austin (UTA), America’s largest university. Clearance for Federal Tax Information, state SPI, etc. Built and maintained public-facing tax systems for TWC. Created UTA's enterprise service bus, frameworks and libraries improving app security and developer productivity, systems preserving legal compliance and accreditation for $600M/yr. of research, public-facing network activation/payment system, among much else.

Boston Computer Society “Excellence” award for Gatekeeper anti-virus system. Expert witness in several gigabuck security software patent lawsuits.

Languages: Java, Javascript (including AJAX), C, etc.
Markup: XML, XHTML, HTML, CSS, Bootstrap, SVG, MathML, LEDES
Build Tools: Maven, Ant, Gradle, Jenkins
Application Servers: Apache Tomcat, JBoss EAP, Amazon Elastic Beanstalk
Frameworks: Spring, also created high security/productivity frameworks for web and SQL: Qwicap and DBTools.
Databases: MySQL, Db2, Oracle SQL, Microsoft SQL Server, Amazon SimpleDB, LDAP

positions.title: Senior Software Engineer
positions.description:
Senior software engineer and architect in research administration.

* Developed, among related tools, an automatic system to help researchers and their staff keep their required training up to date, thus legally safeguarding a significant portion of our $600 million/year in research grants (to say nothing of the valuable research) from legal problems, and/or loss of accreditation.

* Developed web-based tool for data gathering from researchers, and data reduction/reporting for administrators, in order to meet institutional USDA reporting requirements, and maintain research accreditation.

* Financial Interest Disclosure tools, including automated email, and web applications.

positions.title: Senior Software Engineer
positions.description:
Member of “Enterprise Resource Planning” and “Tools” teams of Information Technology Services department’s “Applications” division. Notable projects:

• “XML Gateway” – Mission-critical, high-security enterprise service bus, allowing distributed technologies access to arbitrarily sensitive administrative mainframe data and software. Stores extensive forensic data such that misuse of a service can be fully characterized, allowing any compromised data to be identified, and aiding in tracking of perpetrators. 2003-2011.

• “Qwicap” – High-security/simplicity/productivity open-source web app framework, which serves as the basis for TIM, the ID Photos suite, and the XML Gateway, as well as many small tools, and, potentially, apps around the world. Sole inventor, architect, developer, documenter, etc. 2003-present.

• TIM (“The Identity Manager”) – Java based re-engineering of the campus identity management system. Requested for the project as lead Java developer in order to supply the web and database frameworks (Qwicap and DBTools), develop mission-critical core code, and oversee the work of all other Java developers while assisting them in both solving particular problems and building their Java skills. 2005-2006.

• TAM (“The Access Manager”), an RSA ClearTrust based replacement for the home-grown UT Austin single sign-on system (“Fat Cookie”).

• “DBTools” – SQL framework for MySQL, Oracle and SQL Server. 2005-2015.

• “ID Photos suite” – Photo-based class rosters, virtual ID cards, secure access to ID photos embedded use, and underlying support software. 2010-2011.

• “Document Repository” – A secure, simple, mainframe integrated, centralized document storage/retrieval system upon which numerous departments have built web apps.

• “Heat Map” – Provides “heat map”-style visualizations of campus wireless network use. Aided in justifying and planning the expansion of an enterprise wireless network that had over 2,500 WAPs in 2010.

positions.title: Senior Operating Systems Specialist
positions.description:
Software engineer for “Networking” group of the Computation Center/ACITS/Information Technology Services department and the University of Texas System Office of Telecommunication Services. Notable projects:

• “Pay-Up-Front” – Architected the original version which provided an automatic, and dependable means of collecting fees for services from our clients, and cooperated on the development subsequent versions. The initial version helped move the Computation Center from over $1 million in bad debt to zero in just two years.

• “NetDirect” – Managed access to, and a series of payment models for, both the campus residence hall networks, and the Telesys dial-up system (voted best ISP by Austin Chronicle readers two years running). 1998-2008.

• Texas-Exes Email Forwarding System – Provides permanent email aliases/forwarding to U.T. Austin graduates, while aiding the Exes’ fund-raising efforts.

• “OSW Client Proxy” – Client-side implementation of the OSW encryption and authorization system that allowed secure tn3270 network access to the U.T. Austin administrative mainframe. 1998-2009.

• “Graphlets” – Real-time representations of the status of most any system that logs state information to an SQL database. Real-time data is available as SVG graphs, and discrete text “datums.” 2001-present.

• “Fat Cookie” Java Library – Used by all U.T. Austin Java applications that need the credentials provided by the campus authentication system. To ensure trouble-free usage, the library transparently incorporates years of accumulated knowledge of, and automatic workarounds for, issues like the various cookie corruption bugs in versions of Apache Tomcat. 1998-present.

positions.title: Senior Operating Systems Specialist
positions.description:
Senior Macintosh software engineer and consultant for the Computation Center’s “Microcomputer Technologies” group. Notable projects:

• The campus laser-printing system for Macintoshes (and later PCs), which earned the Computation Center millions of dollars a year for many years, leveraged and increased ROI on existing facilities and equipment, while providing students and faculty easy, economical access to needed high quality Postscript output devices.

• Created U.T. Austin’s first home page and associated web site in 1993, operating on my own initiative. Had the vision and commitment to disobey direct orders to take it down, because “we do Gopher.” The rest is history.

• The “microlib/mac” Internet software archive; originally an FTP site, with the advent of the web it also became the first such site to include a web interface (richly featured, and produced programmatically).

• Provided forensic data preservation and recovery services to U.T. Austin’s Police Department, and its Philosophy Department (rescued the Vlastos archives willed to U.T. Austin).

• Early versions of the “LabMan” software suite that managed access to microcomputers in campus computer labs.

• Produced a variety of utilities, applications, and OS patches for the original Mac OS. Wrote various documentation, hundreds of software reviews, and articles for the nationally distributed Computation Center and MicroGram newsletters.

positions.title: Inventor, Developer, and Everything Else
positions.description: Invented, implemented, distributed and supported the first anti-virus system able to recognize and stop unknown viruses and self-propagating malware. Worked in secret team of academic and industry Macintosh anti-virus researchers and developers to analyze and classify new viruses upon discovery, issue unified press releases to the public, cooperate with law enforcement authorities internationally, and coordinate new releases of all anti-virus tools (commercial, shareware and freeware). Delivered a paper on the state of Macintosh viruses, and our unique response to them, at the Virus Bulletin conference in Edinburgh, Scotland. Our efforts appear to have halted Macintosh virus development (so far).

projects.title: Qwicap
projects.description:
A once possible future for Java web development, Qwicap couldn’t be open-sourced in time to broaden the industry’s perspective enough to burst the pigeonholes of Struts, or prevent its entrapment in the next set of pigeonholes to come along, Spring. The industry said I was wrong (in some respects, so did I), but lack of perspective blinds it to the greater mistakes it embraced.

Since 2018, have been reviewing and revising the code-base (Javadoc and comments included),  moving to a more conventional code-style, improving technical writing, replacing Ant with Maven, adding HTML 5 support, removing legacy complications, increasing unit testing, “teaching” the code lessons I’ve learned since its 2003 inception, and optimizing. In short, there’s an enormous commit coming one of these days. (Yes, where possible, the work should have been a series of ad-hoc commits—and some of it was—but, upon reaching a potential stopping-point, my thoughts are usually of opportunities for related improvements, rather than the opportunity to commit and show incremental progress. Seeing and striking the best balance in the moment is a work-in-progress, like all my skills.)
